title: FTC fines Facebook $5 billion over privacy deception
hook: The largest privacy penalty of its time came from breaking an earlier promise to the regulator.
collected: Profile and friends' data available to third-party apps; phone numbers given for security (two-factor login).
done: The FTC alleged Facebook deceived users about their control over their data, breaking its 2012 FTC order, including letting apps access friends' data and using security phone numbers for advertising.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: FTC order (3-2 vote). No admission of the allegations.

outcome.text: $5 billion penalty, a 20-year order, an independent board privacy committee and quarterly certifications by the CEO.

sources.title: FTC Imposes $5 Billion Penalty and Sweeping New Privacy Restrictions on Facebook

limits: Two commissioners dissented, arguing it was too weak.
whyItMatters: Promises in a privacy policy can be enforced.

title: Cambridge Analytica: a personality quiz harvested friends' data
hook: The deception is documented. Whether 'psychographic' targeting changed votes is not.
collected: Facebook profile data from people who took a quiz app (GSRApp) and from their friends.
howObtained: Facebook's app platform let the quiz see friends' data.
done: The FTC found Cambridge Analytica deceived people about collecting identifiable data. At least 250,000 app users and 50-65 million of their friends were affected, per the FTC.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: FTC opinion and order for the deception. That psychographic targeting was effective is CONTESTED: the UK ICO (2020) found the company's methods "knowingly oversold".

companyResponse.text: Cambridge Analytica was bankrupt and did not respond; its former CEO and the app developer settled with the FTC.

outcome.text: FTC order requiring deletion of data. UK ICO letter (2 October 2020, to Julian Knight MP) found no Facebook data used for Brexit and no evidence of Russian involvement beyond what was known.

sources.title: FTC Sues Cambridge Analytica, Settles with Former CEO and App Developer
UK investigation confirms Cambridge Analytica sought to predict partisanship

limits: We could not open the ICO letter PDF itself.
whyItMatters: Separating what was collected from what was achieved is the core skill of this exhibit.

title: Facebook's emotional contagion experiment
hook: 689,003 people's feeds were tweaked to see if emotions spread. The effect was tiny.
collected: Posts in users' News Feeds and the words users then wrote.
howObtained: Facebook's own platform, for one week in January 2012.
inferred: Whether seeing fewer positive or negative posts changed what people wrote.
done: Researchers reduced positive or negative posts in feeds and measured emotional words in users' own posts. Removing positive posts reduced users' positive words by about 0.1 percentage points (effect size d = 0.02).
affected: 689,003 Facebook users who were not told.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: Peer-reviewed (PNAS). The journal later published an Editorial Expression of Concern about consent. Whether it measured mood rather than word choice is CONTESTED.

companyResponse.text: Lead author Adam Kramer apologised publicly for how the paper described the research.

outcome.text: PNAS Expression of Concern (July 2014) on informed consent and opt-out.

sources.title: Experimental evidence of massive-scale emotional contagion through social networks

limits: Measured words, not feelings. Effects were very small.
whyItMatters: Feeds are tested on you. The ethics matter even when the effect is small.

title: Twitter used security phone numbers and emails for ads ($150 million)
hook: You gave your number to protect your account. It was also used to target ads.
collected: Phone numbers and email addresses provided for account security.
howObtained: Users were asked for them to secure their accounts.
done: The FTC alleged that from 2014 to 2019 Twitter let advertisers target more than 140 million users using contact details given for security.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: FTC/DOJ order. No admission of wrongdoing.

companyResponse.text: Twitter said it had never disclosed or shared phone numbers or email addresses with advertisers.

sources.title: FTC Charges Twitter with Deceptively Using Account Security Data to Sell Targeted Ads

whyItMatters: Data given for one purpose was used for another ('purpose creep').

title: Data about people who never joined
hook: Your friends' uploads can reveal things about you, though weakly.
collected: Contact lists uploaded by users; personal details friends share.
inferred: Information about non-users or about users from others' data.
done: Venkatadri et al. (PETS 2019) showed Facebook used personal details obtained from friends' contact uploads, and phone numbers given for two-factor login, for ad targeting. Garcia (Science Advances, 2017) showed friends' data could predict non-users' traits, but only modestly (AUC about 0.57-0.62, where 0.5 is chance).
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: Peer-reviewed research. Note the weak predictive power in Garcia's study.

companyResponse.text: Mark Zuckerberg told Congress in 2018 that Facebook collects some data on people who have not signed up "for security purposes".

sources.title: Investigating sources of PII used in Facebook's targeted advertising
Leaking privacy and shadow profiles in online social networks

limits: Predictions about non-users are much weaker than headlines suggest.
whyItMatters: Your privacy depends partly on choices other people make.

title: Facebook's ad delivery skewed by gender and race even with neutral targeting
hook: Advertisers chose 'everyone'; the algorithm chose who actually saw the job ad.
collected: Engagement history used by the ad-delivery algorithm.
inferred: Who is most 'relevant' to an ad.
done: Ali et al. (CSCW 2019) ran real ads with identical, neutral targeting and found significant skew in delivery along gender and racial lines, driven by the ad's content and budget.
affected: People who did or did not see job and housing ads.
label: DOCUMENTED

outcome.text: Cited in the 2022 DOJ/HUD settlement with Meta.

sources.title: Discrimination through optimization: How Facebook's ad delivery can lead to skewed outcomes

limits: Measured specific ads at a specific time.
whyItMatters: Discrimination can come from optimisation, with no bad intent from the advertiser.

title: US v. Meta: housing ads settlement
hook: Meta agreed to rebuild how housing ads are delivered.
collected: User data used for ad targeting and delivery.
done: The Justice Department alleged Meta's housing-ad targeting and delivery discriminated in violation of the Fair Housing Act.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: DOJ settlement. No admission of wrongdoing.

outcome.text: Meta paid $115,054 (the legal maximum), dropped the Special Ad Audience tool and built a 'Variance Reduction System' to even out delivery, with compliance targets agreed in January 2023.

sources.title: Justice Department Secures Groundbreaking Settlement Agreement with Meta Platforms
Meta settles lawsuit over housing ads

limits: Applies to housing ads in the US.
whyItMatters: Shows an algorithm being changed by law.

title: Norway fines Grindr: using the app reveals your sexual orientation
hook: Courts agreed that merely being a Grindr user is sensitive data.
collected: GPS location, advertising ID, and the fact of using Grindr.
howObtained: Shared by the app with advertising partners.
done: Norway's data protection authority found Grindr shared users' data with ad-tech partners without valid consent, and that using Grindr reveals sexual orientation, which is special-category data under GDPR.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: Regulator decision, upheld by the Privacy Appeals Board, Oslo District Court and the Borgarting Court of Appeal (21 October 2025).

companyResponse.text: Grindr argued the authority relied on a number of misjudgements.

outcome.text: NOK 65 million fine (about €5.5 million), upheld on appeal. The appeals court also called Grindr's 'we do not sell your personal user information' claim clearly misleading.

sources.title: Borgarting Court of Appeal upheld NOK 65 million fine against Grindr

limits: We could not open the Norwegian authority's original decision.
whyItMatters: An app can reveal something about you just by being on your phone.

title: India bans 59 Chinese apps, including TikTok
hook: The government cited data security and sovereignty; the evidence was not made public.
collected: Per the government: user data from apps such as TikTok.
done: India's IT ministry blocked 59 apps under Section 69A of the IT Act, saying they were "prejudicial to sovereignty and integrity of India" and citing concerns about data security and privacy.
label: STATEMENT
labelNote: The government's stated reasons. No public technical evidence was released; the ban came during a border clash with China.

companyResponse.text: TikTok said it complied with Indian law. We did not find its exact statement in an opened source.

sources.title: Government Bans 59 mobile apps
sources.publisher: Press Information Bureau, Government of India

limits: Reasons are a statement, not a published finding.
whyItMatters: Data protection can also be a geopolitical argument.

title: iOS 14 caught apps reading the clipboard
hook: A new pop-up revealed TikTok and dozens of other apps checking what you had copied.
collected: Whatever was on the clipboard (passwords, messages, links).
howObtained: Apps read the clipboard when opened or while typing.
done: Developers Mysk and Haj Bakry reported more than 50 apps reading the clipboard. Apple's iOS 14 beta added a notification, which showed TikTok reading it every few keystrokes.
label: REPORTED
labelNote: Independent developer research, confirmed in practice by Apple's new warning. TikTok's explanation is a STATEMENT.

companyResponse.text: TikTok said the behaviour came from an anti-spam feature and pushed an update to remove it.

sources.title: Popular iPhone and iPad apps snooping on the pasteboard

limits: Reading the clipboard is not proof the data was sent away.
whyItMatters: Operating-system warnings make hidden behaviour visible.
